question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the 'give-way' vessel?
choice_a: The vessel that has the other on its own starboard (right) side
choice_b: The vessel that has the other on its own port (left) side
explanation: In a crossing situation, the power-driven vessel that has the other vessel on its own starboard side must give way, typically by slowing, stopping, or turning to pass behind the other vessel.

question: In a head-on meeting situation between two power-driven vessels, what should each do?
choice_a: The larger vessel always has right-of-way and continues straight
choice_b: Each vessel should alter course to starboard so they pass port-to-port
choice_c: Each vessel should alter course to port so they pass starboard-to-starboard
choice_d: Neither vessel should change course; they should stop and wait
explanation: When two power-driven vessels meet head-on or nearly so, Navigation Rules direct each to alter course to starboard, resulting in a safe port-to-port passing, similar to cars keeping to the right.

question: What must the 'give-way' vessel do when required to yield right-of-way?
choice_a: Ignore the other vessel and maintain course and speed
choice_b: Only act if a collision is imminent
choice_c: Take early and substantial action to keep well clear of the other vessel
choice_d: Speed up to cross ahead of the other vessel as quickly as possible
explanation: The give-way vessel must take early and obvious action -- slowing, stopping, or altering course -- well before a close-quarters situation develops, rather than waiting until the last moment.
source_note: Navigation Rules, action by give-way vessel (Rule 16)

question: What must the 'stand-on' vessel do in a right-of-way situation?
choice_a: Immediately change course to get out of the way
choice_d: Generally maintain its current course and speed so the give-way vessel can predict its movement and take action to avoid collision
explanation: The stand-on vessel should hold its course and speed to remain predictable, only taking action if it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not acting appropriately or collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel alone.
source_note: Navigation Rules, action by stand-on vessel (Rule 17)

question: In an overtaking situation, which vessel must keep clear of the other?
choice_a: The vessel that is overtaking (coming from behind) must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken
choice_b: The vessel being overtaken must always yield to the faster vessel
choice_d: Overtaking situations are not addressed by Navigation Rules
explanation: The overtaking vessel is always the give-way vessel and must keep clear until it is finally past and clear, regardless of what type of vessel is being overtaken.

question: What is the general right-of-way relationship between a sailboat under sail alone and a power-driven vessel?
choice_a: Sailboats have no right-of-way privileges under any circumstance
choice_b: The sailboat generally has the right-of-way over the power-driven vessel
choice_c: The power-driven vessel always has the right-of-way over a sailboat
choice_d: Right-of-way between sail and power depends only on vessel size
explanation: A sailing vessel under sail alone is generally the stand-on vessel over a power-driven vessel, though a sailboat also under engine power (motor-sailing) is legally considered a power-driven vessel for right-of-way purposes.
source_note: Navigation Rules, sail vs. power-driven priority (Rule 18)

question: How does a sailboat count as a power-driven vessel for right-of-way purposes?
choice_a: Only if the boat has no sails installed at all
choice_c: Whenever it is also being propelled by an engine (motor-sailing), even with the sails up
choice_d: Sailboats are never treated as power-driven vessels under any circumstance
explanation: A sailboat under engine power is legally a power-driven vessel for right-of-way purposes, even if its sails remain up, since the engine -- not the wind -- is providing propulsion.
source_note: Navigation Rules, definition of vessel under sail vs. power

question: What right-of-way priority applies between a power-driven vessel and a vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver (such as one laying cable or dredging)?
choice_a: Restricted vessels must always yield to ordinary power-driven vessels
choice_b: There is no priority difference between the two
choice_c: The faster vessel always has priority
choice_d: The ordinary power-driven vessel must generally give way to the vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver
explanation: Vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver, such as those engaged in dredging or cable-laying, sit higher in the right-of-way hierarchy, and an ordinary power-driven vessel must keep clear of them.

question: What does one short blast of a horn mean when signaling intentions to a nearby vessel under the Inland Navigation Rules?
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my port side (altering course to starboard)
choice_c: I intend to overtake you on your port side
choice_d: Danger -- five or more short blasts
explanation: Under Inland Navigation Rules, one short blast signals an intent to alter course to starboard, leaving the other vessel on the signaling vessel's port side.

question: What does five or more short, rapid blasts of a horn mean?
choice_a: A signal used only when docking
choice_b: A danger or doubt signal, warning that the signaling vessel does not understand the other's intentions or perceives danger
choice_d: A request to overtake on the port side
explanation: Five or more short, rapid blasts is the danger signal, used when a vessel doubts the intentions of another vessel or believes a collision risk exists.

question: What sound signal must a power-driven vessel make in conditions of restricted visibility (such as fog)?
choice_a: Continuous horn blasts with no pause
choice_b: A single short blast only once at the start of the fog
choice_c: One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than two minutes
choice_d: No signal is required in fog
explanation: In restricted visibility, a power-driven vessel making way must sound one prolonged blast at intervals of not more than two minutes to alert nearby traffic of its presence.
source_note: Navigation Rules, restricted visibility sound signals (Rule 35)

question: Do canoes, kayaks, and other human-powered vessels have to follow Navigation Rules when interacting with motorized vessels?
choice_a: No, human-powered vessels are exempt from all navigation rules
choice_b: Only powerboats need to follow right-of-way rules
choice_c: Kayaks always have absolute right-of-way over every other vessel type with no exception
choice_d: Yes -- Navigation Rules apply to all vessels, and a vessel under oars/paddles is generally treated similarly to a sailing vessel in the priority order relative to power-driven vessels
explanation: Navigation Rules apply to every vessel on the water, and a vessel under oars or paddles generally ranks similarly to a sailing vessel in the give-way/stand-on hierarchy relative to ordinary power-driven vessels.
source_note: Navigation Rules, applicability to all vessel types
